specStatements.text: In solving quantitative problems, students should be able to recall and apply the following equations, using standard SI units.
Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
Equation 1: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g) [symbol equation: W = m g]
Equation 2: work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force) [symbol equation: W = F s]
Equation 3: force applied to a spring = spring constant × extension [symbol equation: F = k e]
Equation 4: moment of a force = force × distance (normal to direction of force) [symbol equation: M = F d]
Equation 5: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface) [symbol equation: p = F/A]
Equation 6: distance travelled = speed × time [symbol equation: s = v t]
Equation 7: acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken) [symbol equation: a = (∆v)/(t)]
Equation 8: resultant force = mass × acceleration [symbol equation: F = m a]
Equation 9: momentum = mass × velocity [symbol equation: p = m v]
Equation 10: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)^2 [symbol equation: E_k = 1/2m v^2]
Equation 11: gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength (g) × height [symbol equation: E_p = m g h]
Equation 12: power = (energy transferred)/(time) [symbol equation: P = E/t]
Equation 13: power = (work done)/(time) [symbol equation: P = W/t]
Equation 14: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer)
Equation 15: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input)
Equation 16: wave speed = frequency × wavelength [symbol equation: v = f λ]
Equation 17: charge flow = current × time [symbol equation: Q = I t]
Equation 18: potential difference = current × resistance [symbol equation: V = I R]
Equation 19: power = potential difference × current [symbol equation: P = V I]
Equation 20: power = (current)^2 × resistance [symbol equation: P = I^2 R]
Equation 21: energy transferred = power × time [symbol equation: E = P t]
Equation 22: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference [symbol equation: E = Q V]
Equation 23: density = (mass)/(volume) [symbol equation: ρ = m/V]
Students should be able to select and apply the following equations from the Physics equation sheet.
Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
Equation 1: pressure due to a column of liquid = height of column × density of liquid × gravitational field strength (g) [symbol equation: p = h ρ g]
Equation 2: (final velocity)^2 –(initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance [symbol equation: v^2 –u^2 = 2 a s]
Equation 3: force = (change in momentum)/(time taken) [symbol equation: F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)]
Equation 4: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2 [symbol equation: E_e = 1/2 k e^2]
Equation 5: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change [symbol equation: ∆E = m c ∆θ]
Equation 6: period = (1)/(frequency)
Equation 7: magnification = (image height)/(object height)
Equation 8: force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current = magnetic flux density × current × length [symbol equation: F = B I l]
Equation 9: thermal energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat [symbol equation: E = m L]

Equation 10: (potential difference across primary coil)/(potential difference across secondary coil) = (number of turns in primary coil)/(number of turns in secondary coil) [symbol equation: (V_p)/(V_s) = (n_p)/(n_s)]
Equation 11: potential difference across primary coil × current in primary coil = potential difference across secondary coil × current in secondary coil [symbol equation: V_p I_p = V_s I_s]
Equation 12: For gases: pressure × volume = constant [symbol equation: p V = constant]

scopeNotes.statement: Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: In the recall list the only HT equation is momentum = mass x velocity (p = m v). Its concept, its misconceptions and its question are all tagged tier 'higher'; every other recall item is tagged 'both' and none of them needs an HT-only equation.

scopeNotes.statement: Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: On the equation sheet the HT flag falls on p = h ρ g, F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), F = B I l, V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s and V_p I_p = V_s I_s. Every item built on those five equations is tagged 'higher'; the remaining sheet items are tagged 'both', so no Foundation Tier item requires an HT-only equation.

concepts.definition: One of the 23 equations in the first Appendix A list. It is not printed on any equation sheet, so a student must write it from memory, substitute values and rearrange it when solving quantitative problems.

The unit the Appendix A equations assume: kilogram for mass, metre for length, second for time, and so on. Values given in grams, centimetres, minutes or hours are converted to SI units before substitution.
The letters HT beside an equation in the left hand column, marking an equation that only Higher Tier papers can require. Foundation Tier papers do not ask for it.
The force acting on a mass because of a gravitational field, found from weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g), W = m g, and measured in newtons.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object along the line of action of that force, given by work done = force x distance, W = F s, measured in joules.
The stiffness of a spring, k in force applied to a spring = spring constant x extension, F = k e. Extension is the increase in length, not the total length.
The turning effect of a force about a pivot, moment of a force = force x distance (normal to direction of force), M = F d, in newton metres.
Force acting normally per unit area of a surface: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), p = F/A, in pascals.
The rate at which distance is covered, used as distance travelled = speed x time, s = v t, with distance in metres and time in seconds.
The rate of change of velocity, acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), a = (∆v)/(t), measured in metres per second squared.
The single force equivalent to all the forces on an object. Only the resultant force is used in resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a.
A property of a moving object given by momentum = mass x velocity, p = m v, measured in kilogram metres per second. It is a Higher Tier recall equation.
The energy of a moving object, kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2, E_k = 1/2 m v^2. The speed is squared but the mass is not.
Energy stored by raising a mass in a gravitational field, gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength (g) x height, E_p = m g h.
The rate of energy transfer, power = (energy transferred)/(time), P = E/t, measured in watts. One watt is one joule per second.
The rate of doing work, power = (work done)/(time), P = W/t. It gives the same value as P = E/t because work done is energy transferred.
The fraction of the energy supplied that is usefully transferred: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). It has no unit and cannot exceed 1.
The same ratio expressed using power: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). It is used when powers rather than energies are given.
The speed at which a wave transfers energy, wave speed = frequency x wavelength, v = f λ, with frequency in hertz and wavelength in metres.
The quantity of charge moved by a current in a time, charge flow = current x time, Q = I t, in coulombs.
The opposition of a component to current, appearing in potential difference = current x resistance, V = I R, with resistance in ohms.
The rate of energy transfer in a circuit, power = potential difference x current, P = V I.
Power calculated from current and resistance alone: power = (current)^2 x resistance, P = I^2 R. The current is squared, not the resistance.
Energy found from energy transferred = power x time, E = P t, with power in watts and time in seconds.
Energy found from energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, E = Q V, with charge in coulombs.
Mass per unit volume, density = (mass)/(volume), ρ = m/V, in kilograms per cubic metre when SI units are used.
One of the 12 equations printed on the Physics equation sheet. It does not have to be recalled, but the right one must be selected and applied correctly.
The HT marking on the equation sheet list, showing which of the printed equations only Higher Tier papers can require.
Pressure due to a column of liquid = height of column x density of liquid x gravitational field strength (g), p = h ρ g. It depends on depth, not on the width of the container.
(final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 x acceleration x distance, v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s, used when time is not known.
Force expressed as force = (change in momentum)/(time taken), F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). A longer impact time gives a smaller force for the same change in momentum.
Energy stored in a stretched spring, elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
The constant c in change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change, ∆E = m c ∆θ: the energy needed to raise one kilogram by one degree.
The time for one complete wave or oscillation, period = (1)/(frequency), measured in seconds.
A ratio found from magnification = (image height)/(object height). Because it is a ratio of two lengths it has no unit.
The quantity B in force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current = magnetic flux density x current x length, F = B I l, measured in tesla.
The constant L in thermal energy for a change of state = mass x specific latent heat, E = m L: the energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change.
The relation (potential difference across primary coil)/(potential difference across secondary coil) = (number of turns in primary coil)/(number of turns in secondary coil), V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s.

For a transformer assumed to be 100% efficient, potential difference across primary coil x current in primary coil = potential difference across secondary coil x current in secondary coil, V_p I_p = V_s I_s.
For gases: pressure x volume = constant, p V = constant, at constant temperature for a fixed mass of gas.

misconceptions.question: A mass is given as 250 g. What is substituted into an Appendix A equation?
misconceptions.correct: 0.25 kg, because the equations are applied in standard SI units.
misconceptions.misconception: Whatever number the question prints is the number that goes into the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Substitution is treated as copying digits, with the unit seen as a label added afterwards rather than part of the quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Convert to SI units first: grams to kilograms, centimetres to metres, minutes to seconds. The answer then comes out in the SI unit too.

misconceptions.question: A time is given as 2.0 minutes. What is substituted?
misconceptions.correct: 120 s, because the SI unit of time is the second.
misconceptions.misconception: A time is a time, so 2.0 goes in whatever the unit says.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Time feels like a familiar everyday quantity, so the minute is not recognised as a non-SI unit needing conversion.
misconceptions.correction: Times must be converted to seconds before substitution; 2.0 minutes is 120 s.

misconceptions.question: A mass of 250 g is converted for use in W = m g. What is the risk?
misconceptions.correct: Writing 250 kg instead of 0.25 kg by changing the label and not the number.
misconceptions.misconception: Changing g to kg just means writing kg after the same number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Unit conversion is remembered as a relabelling rule rather than a division or multiplication by 1000.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing by 1000 changes the number as well as the unit: 250 g becomes 0.25 kg.

misconceptions.question: What does HT beside an Appendix A equation mean?
misconceptions.correct: Only Higher Tier papers can require that equation.
misconceptions.misconception: HT is just a note that the equation is harder, so everyone still needs it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The letters are read as a difficulty warning rather than as a tier label defining what each paper can ask.
misconceptions.correction: HT marks the tier: Foundation Tier papers cannot require an HT equation, Higher Tier papers can.

misconceptions.question: How is the weight of a 6.0 kg mass found on Earth?
misconceptions.correct: weight = mass x gravitational field strength, so W = 6.0 x 9.8 N.
misconceptions.misconception: The weight is 6.0 N because weight and mass are the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language uses 'weight' for what is measured in kilograms, so the two quantities are merged.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is in kilograms and does not change; weight is a force in newtons found from W = m g.

misconceptions.question: Which quantity is g in W = m g?
misconceptions.correct: The gravitational field strength at that place.
misconceptions.misconception: g is the acceleration of the object, so W = m g only works while falling.
misconceptions.whyItArises: W = m g and F = m a look identical, so g is read as an acceleration that must be happening now.
misconceptions.correction: g is the gravitational field strength. A stationary object still has weight m g.

misconceptions.question: A force of 12 N drags a box 0.50 m along the line of the force. What is the work done?
misconceptions.correct: 6 J, from work done = force x distance.
misconceptions.misconception: Work done is force divided by distance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Per' language from pressure and density is carried over to work, where nothing is divided.
misconceptions.correction: W = F s multiplies the force by the distance moved along the line of action of the force.

misconceptions.question: A distance is given as 50 cm in a work calculation. What is used?
misconceptions.correct: 0.50 m, converted to the SI unit of length.
misconceptions.misconception: The number 50 can go straight into W = F s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The centimetre is so familiar that it is not registered as a non-SI unit.
misconceptions.correction: Convert centimetres to metres by dividing by 100 before substituting.

misconceptions.question: A spring 30 cm long stretches to 35 cm under a force. What is e in F = k e?
misconceptions.correct: 0.05 m, the extension, which is the increase in length.
misconceptions.misconception: e is the length of the stretched spring, so e = 0.35 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Extension' is read as 'how long it is now' rather than 'how much longer it has become'.
misconceptions.correction: Extension is final length minus original length, converted to metres.

misconceptions.question: A spring constant is 15 N/m and the extension is 5.0 cm. What is the force?
misconceptions.correct: 0.75 N, using e = 0.05 m.
misconceptions.misconception: The force is 75 N, using the extension as 5.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Numbers are substituted in the units printed in the question rather than in metres.
misconceptions.correction: Convert the extension to metres first: 5.0 cm is 0.05 m, giving 0.75 N.

misconceptions.question: A car travels at 15 m/s for 4.0 s. What distance is covered?
misconceptions.correct: 60 m, from distance travelled = speed x time.
misconceptions.misconception: 3.75 m, because distance is speed divided by time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled as a triangle and the wrong pair is read off it.
misconceptions.correction: s = v t multiplies speed by time; dividing gives neither a distance nor sensible units.

misconceptions.question: A car speeds up from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 8.0 s. What is the acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 0.75 m/s2, using the change in velocity of 6 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: 1.3 m/s2, using the final velocity of 10 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as velocity over time, so the initial velocity is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: a = (∆v)/(t) uses the change in velocity: final minus initial.

misconceptions.question: How is a = (∆v)/(t) applied?
misconceptions.correct: The change in velocity is divided by the time taken.
misconceptions.misconception: The change in velocity is multiplied by the time taken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acceleration is loosely described as speed 'building up over time', which suggests multiplying.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is a rate, so the change in velocity is divided by the time it took.

misconceptions.question: Which force is F in F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: The resultant force on the object.
misconceptions.misconception: Any one of the forces named in the question.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Questions often give several forces, and the first one quoted is taken as F.
misconceptions.correction: F = m a uses the resultant force, found by combining all the forces acting.

misconceptions.question: How is the momentum of a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s found?
misconceptions.correct: 6.0 kg m/s, from momentum = mass x velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: 9.0 units, because the velocity is squared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Momentum and kinetic energy both involve mass and velocity, so the squared term is carried across.
misconceptions.correction: p = m v has no square. Only kinetic energy squares the speed.

misconceptions.question: A 4.0 kg mass moves at 3.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
misconceptions.misconception: 36 J, from mass x speed squared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The one half is treated as decoration and dropped when the sum is written out.
misconceptions.correction: E_k = 1/2 m v^2 includes the factor of one half.

misconceptions.question: Which quantity is squared in E_k = 1/2 m v^2?
misconceptions.correct: The speed only.
misconceptions.misconception: Both the mass and the speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The square is attached to the whole expression rather than to v alone.
misconceptions.correction: Only the speed is squared; doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy but doubling the speed quadruples it.

misconceptions.question: A 2.0 kg bag is carried 5.0 m up a ramp, rising 3.0 m. Which height is used in E_p = m g h?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 m, the vertical height gained.
misconceptions.misconception: 5.0 m, the distance moved along the ramp.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only length noticed is the one the object travelled along.
misconceptions.correction: h in E_p = m g h is the vertical height, not the distance along a slope.

misconceptions.question: How is gravitational potential energy calculated for a mass of 3.0 kg raised 2.0 m?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 x 9.8 x 2.0, from E_p = m g h.
misconceptions.misconception: By multiplying weight by g by height.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Weight is already m g, but g is written in again from memory of the formula.
misconceptions.correction: Use mass x g x height, or equivalently weight x height. Using g twice doubles the answer wrongly.

misconceptions.question: A device transfers 6000 J in 30 s. What is its power?
misconceptions.correct: 200 W, from power = (energy transferred)/(time).
misconceptions.misconception: 180000 W, from energy multiplied by time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power is described as energy 'over time', which is read as energy across a period rather than a division.
misconceptions.correction: P = E/t divides the energy transferred by the time taken.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between energy transferred and power?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is measured in joules; power is the rate of transfer, in watts.
misconceptions.misconception: They are the same thing measured in different units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are quoted for appliances, and joules and watts are used loosely in adverts.
misconceptions.correction: Power tells you how fast energy is transferred: one watt is one joule each second.

misconceptions.question: A machine does 900 J of work in 45 s. What is the power?
misconceptions.correct: 20 W, from power = (work done)/(time).
misconceptions.misconception: 0.05 W, from time divided by work done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The fraction is inverted when the equation is written from memory.
misconceptions.correction: P = W/t puts the work done on top and the time underneath.

misconceptions.question: A motor is supplied with 500 J and usefully transfers 300 J. What is its efficiency?
misconceptions.correct: 0.6, from useful output divided by total input.
misconceptions.misconception: 1.67, from total input divided by useful output.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The larger number is instinctively placed on top so that the answer looks tidier.
misconceptions.correction: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer), so the useful output goes on top.

misconceptions.question: A lamp wastes 80 J and usefully transfers 20 J from 100 J supplied. What is the efficiency?
misconceptions.correct: 0.2, using the 20 J usefully transferred.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.8, using the 80 J wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The bigger energy figure is assumed to be the important one.
misconceptions.correction: Only the useful output energy transfer goes on top of the efficiency fraction.

misconceptions.question: A pump has a total power input of 400 W and a useful power output of 250 W. What is its efficiency?
misconceptions.correct: 0.625, from useful power output over total power input.
misconceptions.misconception: 1.6, from total power input over useful power output.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The efficiency fraction is written down without checking which power belongs on top.
misconceptions.correction: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input); the answer can never be greater than 1.

misconceptions.question: Can an efficiency come out greater than 1?
misconceptions.correct: No, because the useful output can never exceed the total input.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, if the machine is a very good one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Efficiency is remembered as a score rather than as a fraction of the energy supplied.
misconceptions.correction: An answer above 1 means the fraction has been written upside down.

misconceptions.question: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. What is its speed?
misconceptions.correct: 300 m/s, from wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
misconceptions.misconception: 8.3 m/s, from frequency divided by wavelength.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed is associated with dividing, as in speed = distance over time.
misconceptions.correction: v = f λ multiplies the frequency by the wavelength.

misconceptions.question: A wavelength is given as 20 cm. What is used in v = f λ?
misconceptions.misconception: 20, because the wavelength is already a number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Wavelengths are often drawn in centimetres on diagrams, so the unit is not questioned.
misconceptions.correction: Convert the wavelength to metres so the speed comes out in metres per second.

misconceptions.question: A current of 3.0 A flows for 40 s. What charge flows?
misconceptions.correct: 120 C, from charge flow = current x time.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.075 C, from current divided by time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge and current are both described in terms of flow, so the relationship is guessed.
misconceptions.correction: Q = I t multiplies the current by the time.

misconceptions.question: A current flows for 2.0 minutes. What time is used in Q = I t?
misconceptions.misconception: 2.0, because the equation just needs the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ampere is not recognised as a coulomb per second, so seconds are not required.
misconceptions.correction: Time must be in seconds, since one ampere is one coulomb per second.

misconceptions.question: A 6.0 V supply drives 0.50 A through a resistor. What is its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: 12 ohms, by rearranging V = I R.
misconceptions.misconception: 3.0 ohms, from potential difference multiplied by current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rearrangement is guessed because V = I R is only remembered in one form.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V/I, so divide the potential difference by the current.

misconceptions.question: How is the current found from V = I R?
misconceptions.correct: By dividing the potential difference by the resistance.
misconceptions.misconception: By multiplying the potential difference by the resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Multiplication is the operation seen in the printed form of the equation, so it is repeated.
misconceptions.correction: I = V/R. A larger resistance gives a smaller current for the same potential difference.

misconceptions.question: A device works at 230 V and draws 2.0 A. What is its power?
misconceptions.correct: 460 W, from power = potential difference x current.
misconceptions.misconception: 115 W, from potential difference divided by current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: P = V I is confused with the many equations in this list that are fractions.
misconceptions.correction: P = V I is a product of the potential difference and the current.

misconceptions.question: A current of 3.0 A passes through a 4.0 ohm resistor. What power is dissipated?
misconceptions.correct: 36 W, from power = (current)^2 x resistance.
misconceptions.misconception: 48 W, from current times resistance squared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The square is attached to the nearer symbol when the equation is written from memory.
misconceptions.correction: P = I^2 R squares the current, not the resistance.

misconceptions.question: A 2000 W heater runs for 300 s. What energy is transferred?
misconceptions.correct: 600000 J, from energy transferred = power x time.
misconceptions.misconception: 6.7 J, from power divided by time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy and power are not clearly separated, so the operation is chosen at random.
misconceptions.correction: E = P t multiplies the power by the time in seconds.

misconceptions.question: An appliance is used for half an hour. What time is used in E = P t?
misconceptions.misconception: 0.5, the number of hours given.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electricity bills use kilowatt-hours, so hours feel like an acceptable unit here.
misconceptions.correction: Standard SI units are required, so convert the time to seconds to get an answer in joules.

misconceptions.question: A charge of 30 C moves through a potential difference of 12 V. What energy is transferred?
misconceptions.correct: 360 J, from energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: 2.5 J, from charge divided by potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled as a fraction because so many electrical equations are fractions.
misconceptions.correction: E = Q V multiplies the charge flow by the potential difference.

misconceptions.question: A block of mass 240 kg has a volume of 0.30 m3. What is its density?
misconceptions.correct: 800 kg/m3, from density = (mass)/(volume).
misconceptions.misconception: 0.00125 kg/m3, from volume divided by mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The fraction is written down the wrong way when the equation is recalled quickly.
misconceptions.correction: ρ = m/V puts the mass on top and the volume underneath.

misconceptions.question: A volume is given as 500 cm3. What is used in ρ = m/V?
misconceptions.correct: 0.0005 m3, the volume in cubic metres.
misconceptions.misconception: 500, because a volume is a volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Converting a cubed unit needs division by 1000000, which is easy to forget.
misconceptions.correction: 1 m3 is 1000000 cm3, so divide by a million to reach standard SI units.

misconceptions.question: What must be done with the equations on the Physics equation sheet?
misconceptions.correct: Select the right one and apply it; they do not have to be recalled.
misconceptions.misconception: Every equation in Appendix A must be memorised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two Appendix A lists look alike, so the difference between them is missed.
misconceptions.correction: The first list must be recalled; the second is printed on the sheet and must be selected and applied.

misconceptions.question: Which sheet equations carry the HT flag?
misconceptions.correct: p = h ρ g, F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), F = B I l and the two transformer equations.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything printed on the sheet is Higher Tier only.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sheet is seen as an extra for harder papers rather than as a resource for both tiers.
misconceptions.correction: Both tiers use the sheet. Only the equations marked HT are restricted to Higher Tier papers.

misconceptions.question: Is v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s a Higher Tier only equation?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is on the sheet without an HT flag, so both tiers may use it.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything with a square in it must be Higher Tier.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Difficulty of appearance is used as the test rather than the printed HT marking.
misconceptions.correction: The HT marking in the left hand column is the only thing that restricts an equation to Higher Tier.

misconceptions.question: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 15 m/s. What is v^2 - u^2?
misconceptions.whyItArises: The velocities are subtracted first because the bracket is read before the index.
misconceptions.correction: Each velocity is squared before subtracting: v^2 - u^2 is not (v - u)^2.

misconceptions.question: What is missing if v^2 - u^2 is set equal to a s?
misconceptions.correct: The factor of 2 on the right hand side.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing; the 2 only applies when the object starts from rest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 2 looks like a detail and is dropped when the equation is copied from memory.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s in all cases.

misconceptions.question: Water at 20 C is heated to 80 C. What value is used for ∆θ?
misconceptions.correct: 60 C, the temperature change.
misconceptions.misconception: 80 C, the final temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final temperature is the number the question ends on, so it is the one remembered.
misconceptions.correction: ∆θ is the temperature change: final temperature minus starting temperature.

misconceptions.question: A mass in a ∆E = m c ∆θ calculation is given as 500 g. What is used?
misconceptions.misconception: 500, since specific heat capacity is per gram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Specific heat capacity is quoted per kilogram, but the unit is not read carefully.
misconceptions.correction: Specific heat capacity is energy per kilogram per degree, so the mass must be in kilograms.

misconceptions.question: A wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its period?
misconceptions.correct: 0.004 s, from period = (1)/(frequency).
misconceptions.misconception: 250 s, because the period and the frequency are the same number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Period and frequency are both described as timing the wave, so they are treated as one idea.
misconceptions.correction: They are reciprocals: a high frequency means a short period.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the period when the frequency is doubled?
misconceptions.correct: It halves.
misconceptions.misconception: It doubles as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities describe how fast the wave oscillates, so they are assumed to change together.
misconceptions.correction: period = (1)/(frequency), so doubling the frequency halves the period.

misconceptions.question: A current of 3.0 A passes through a 4.0 ohm resistor. What power is dissipated?
misconceptions.correct: 36 W, because the current is squared first.
misconceptions.misconception: The current and the resistance are simply multiplied, giving 12 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: P = I^2 R is remembered as a product, and the index on I is not noticed.
misconceptions.correction: The current must be squared before multiplying by the resistance.

misconceptions.question: 0.25 kg of ice is melted. The specific latent heat of fusion is 334 000 J/kg. What energy is needed?
misconceptions.correct: 83 500 J, from E = m L.
misconceptions.misconception: 334 000 J, the value of the specific latent heat itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The large printed number looks like the answer, so the mass is never used.
misconceptions.correction: The specific latent heat is the energy per kilogram, so it must be multiplied by the mass.

misconceptions.question: How is E = m L used when the mass is less than one kilogram?
misconceptions.correct: The latent heat is multiplied by the mass, giving a smaller energy.
misconceptions.misconception: The latent heat is divided by the mass, since the mass is small.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A mass below one seems to call for division so that the answer looks bigger.
misconceptions.correction: Multiplying by a mass less than one kilogram correctly gives less energy than L.

misconceptions.question: A block of mass 240 kg has a volume of 0.30 m3. What is its density?
misconceptions.correct: 800 kg/m3, from mass divided by volume.
misconceptions.misconception: 72 kg/m3, from the mass multiplied by the volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two quantities are given, so they are combined by multiplying, the more familiar operation.
misconceptions.correction: Density is mass per unit volume, so the mass is divided by the volume.

mcqs.stem: A question gives a mass of 250 g and a time of 2.0 minutes. Which pair of values should be substituted so that the working is in standard SI units?

options.text: a mass of 0.25 kg and a time of 120 s
options.rationale: 250 g is 0.25 kg and 2.0 minutes is 120 s, the SI units of mass and time.

options.text: a mass of 250 g and a time of 2 minutes
options.rationale: The figures are copied straight from the question with no conversion at all.

options.text: a mass of 250 kg and a time of 120 s
options.rationale: The time is converted but the gram figure is simply relabelled as kilograms.

options.text: a mass of 0.25 kg and a time of 2 s
options.rationale: The mass is converted but the minutes are treated as though they were seconds.

mcqs.stem: In the first Appendix A list, what does HT in the left hand column tell you about an equation?

options.text: Both tiers need it, but Higher Tier asks more often
options.rationale: HT is read as a comment on how often the equation appears rather than as a tier limit.

options.text: It is harder to rearrange than the equations near it
options.rationale: The letters are taken as a difficulty warning instead of a tier label.

options.text: Only Higher Tier papers can require that equation
options.rationale: HT marks the equations that Foundation Tier papers cannot ask for.

options.text: It is printed for you on the equation sheet
options.rationale: The HT flag is confused with the separate list of equations given on the sheet.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the Appendix A equation for the weight of an object?

options.text: weight = mass x acceleration of the object
options.rationale: W = m g is confused with F = m a, so g is read as an acceleration of the object.

options.text: weight = mass x gravitational field strength
options.rationale: This is Equation 1, W = m g, with weight in newtons and mass in kilograms.

options.text: weight = mass, because mass is the same as weight
options.rationale: Treating weight and mass as identical, the student writes weight = mass with no field strength.

options.text: weight = mass x field strength x height
options.rationale: The weight equation has been merged with E_p = m g h.

mcqs.stem: A force of 12 N drags a crate 0.50 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done?

options.rationale: The force has been divided by the distance instead of multiplied by it.
The distance has been used as 50 cm rather than converted to 0.50 m.
The force and the distance have been added rather than multiplied.
work done = force x distance, so W = 12 x 0.50 = 6 J.

mcqs.stem: A spring of natural length 30 cm is stretched to 35 cm. The spring constant is 15 N/m. What force is applied to the spring?

options.rationale: The stretched length of 0.35 m has been used in place of the extension.
The extension is 5.0 cm, or 0.05 m, so F = k e = 15 x 0.05 = 0.75 N.
The extension has been left in centimetres instead of being converted to metres.
The spring constant has been divided by the extension in centimetres.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist travels at a steady 15 m/s for 4.0 s. What distance is travelled?

options.rationale: The speed has been divided by the time instead of multiplied by it.
The time has been divided by the speed, inverting the equation.
distance travelled = speed x time, so s = 15 x 4.0 = 60 m.
The multiplication has slipped by a factor of ten.

mcqs.stem: A car speeds up from 4.0 m/s to 10 m/s in 8.0 s. What is its acceleration?

options.rationale: The final velocity of 10 m/s has been used instead of the change in velocity.
The change in velocity has been multiplied by the time rather than divided by it.
The change in velocity is 6.0 m/s, so a = 6.0/8.0 = 0.75 m/s².
This is the change in velocity itself, with no division by the time taken.

mcqs.stem: A box is pushed with a force of 30 N while friction of 12 N acts backwards on it. Which force is used in F = m a?

options.text: the resultant force, which is 18 N
options.rationale: F = m a uses the resultant force, here 30 N minus 12 N.

options.text: the 30 N pushing force applied to the box
options.rationale: The first force named in the question is taken as F.

options.text: the 12 N force of friction on its own
options.rationale: One of the individual forces is used rather than their resultant.

options.text: the two forces added, giving 42 N
options.rationale: The forces are added even though they act in opposite directions.

mcqs.stem: A 1.0 kg mass moves at 4.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.rationale: The factor of one half has been left out of the calculation.
The speed has not been squared, so 0.5 x 1.0 x 4.0 has been worked out.
This is the momentum m v rather than the kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: A 2.0 kg bag is carried 5.0 m up a ramp and ends 3.0 m above its starting level. Taking g = 9.8 N/kg, what is the gain in gravitational potential energy?

options.rationale: The 5.0 m measured along the ramp has been used instead of the vertical height.
The weight has been multiplied by g again, so g has been counted twice.
The gravitational field strength has been left out altogether.
E_p = m g h = 2.0 x 9.8 x 3.0 = 58.8 J, using the vertical height.

mcqs.stem: An electric heater transfers 6000 J of energy in 30 s. Which statement about its power is correct?

options.text: Its power is 180 000 W, from energy times time
options.rationale: The energy has been multiplied by the time instead of divided by it.

options.text: Its power is 200 W, from the energy over time
Its power is 0.005 W, from the time over the energy
options.rationale: The fraction has been written upside down.

options.text: Its power is 6000 W, the energy transferred
options.rationale: Energy and power are treated as the same quantity.

mcqs.stem: A motor does 900 J of work in 45 s. What is its power output, and why?

options.text: 40 500 W, because power is work done times time
options.rationale: The work done has been multiplied by the time rather than divided by it.

options.text: 0.05 W, because power is time divided by work done
options.rationale: The fraction has been inverted when the equation was recalled.

options.text: 20 W, because power is work done divided by time
options.rationale: P = W/t gives 900/45 = 20 W.

options.text: 900 W, since work done and power are the same
options.rationale: Work done in joules is quoted as though it were a power in watts.

mcqs.stem: A motor is supplied with 500 J and usefully transfers 300 J, wasting 200 J. What is its efficiency?

options.text: 0.6, from the useful 300 J divided by the 500 J input
options.rationale: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer.

options.text: 1.5, since a good motor can be more than 100% efficient
options.rationale: Believing efficiency can exceed 1, the student accepts 1.5 as a valid value.

options.text: 0.4, from the wasted 200 J divided by the input
options.rationale: The wasted energy has been treated as the useful output.

options.text: 1.67, from the 500 J input divided by 300 J
options.rationale: The fraction has been inverted, giving an efficiency greater than one.

mcqs.stem: A pump has a total power input of 400 W and a useful power output of 250 W. What is its efficiency?

options.text: 1.6, from the total input divided by the useful output
options.rationale: The ratio has been written upside down, which cannot give a real efficiency.

options.text: 0.375, from the 150 W wasted power over the input
options.rationale: The wasted power has been used in place of the useful output.

options.text: 0.625, from the useful output divided by the total input
options.rationale: efficiency = useful power output / total power input = 250/400.

options.text: 150 W, the difference between the two power values
options.rationale: Efficiency has been treated as a power rather than as a ratio.

mcqs.stem: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz and a wavelength of 400 cm. What is its wave speed?

options.rationale: The wavelength has been left in centimetres instead of converted to metres.
The wavelength is 4.00 m, so v = f λ = 25 x 4.00 = 100 m/s.
The frequency has been divided by the wavelength instead of multiplied by it.
The frequency and the wavelength have been added together.

mcqs.stem: A current of 3.0 A flows for 2.0 minutes. What charge flows?

options.rationale: The time has been left in minutes instead of converted to seconds.
The current has been divided by the time in seconds.
The time has been divided by the current, inverting the equation.
Q = I t with the time converted to 120 s gives 3.0 x 120 = 360 C.

mcqs.stem: A 6.0 V supply drives a current of 0.50 A through a resistor. What is its resistance?

options.rationale: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V/I = 6.0/0.50 = 12 Ω.
The potential difference has been multiplied by the current.
The current has been divided by the potential difference.
The two given values have been added together.

mcqs.stem: A torch bulb works at 4.5 V and draws a current of 0.20 A. What is its power?

options.rationale: The potential difference has been divided by the current.
The current has been divided by the potential difference.
The two values have been added instead of multiplied.

mcqs.stem: A current of 3.0 A passes through a resistor of resistance 4.0 Ω. Which working gives the power dissipated?

options.rationale: The resistance has been squared instead of the current.
Neither quantity has been squared, so only I R has been worked out.
Both the current and the resistance have been squared.
P = I² R squares the current before multiplying by the resistance.

mcqs.stem: A 2000 W heater is switched on for 5.0 minutes. How much energy is transferred?

options.rationale: The time has been left in minutes rather than converted to seconds.
The power has been divided by the time instead of multiplied by it.
E = P t with the time as 300 s gives 2000 x 300 = 600 000 J.
The power has been divided by the time in minutes.

mcqs.stem: A charge of 8.0 C moves through a potential difference of 12 V. How much energy is transferred?

options.rationale: The charge has been divided by the potential difference.
The potential difference has been divided by the charge.
The charge in coulombs has been quoted as though it were the energy.

mcqs.stem: A block of mass 240 kg has a volume of 0.30 m³. What is its density?

options.rationale: The mass has been multiplied by the volume rather than divided by it.
density = mass / volume = 240/0.30 = 800 kg/m³.
The volume has been divided by the mass, inverting the equation.
The place value of the volume has been lost, dividing 24 by 3.

mcqs.stem: How should a student treat the twelve equations in the second Appendix A list?

options.text: Recall them from memory, as with the first list of equations
options.rationale: The two Appendix A lists look alike, so the difference between them is missed.

options.text: Memorise them as well, since none can be looked up
options.rationale: Believing every equation must be memorised, the student says these too must be learned.

options.text: Select the right one from the equation sheet and apply it
options.rationale: These equations are printed on the Physics equation sheet, so they are selected rather than recalled.

options.text: Learn only the ones that are not marked HT in the list
options.rationale: The HT flag is read as deciding what must be learned rather than which tier may be asked.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the HT flags on the Physics equation sheet is correct?

options.text: Higher Tier papers alone can require those equations
options.rationale: The flag restricts the tier, not the availability of the sheet.

options.text: Every equation printed on the equation sheet is HT only
options.rationale: The sheet is seen as an extra for harder papers rather than a resource for both tiers.

options.text: They mark the sheet equations that must also be recalled
options.rationale: The flag is confused with the recall requirement of the first list.

options.text: They mark the equations that contain a square or ratio
options.rationale: Appearance is used as the test rather than the printed marking.

mcqs.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from 5.0 m/s to 15 m/s over a distance of 50 m. Which working gives its acceleration?

options.rationale: The velocities have been subtracted before squaring.
The factor of 2 on the right hand side has been left out.
Neither velocity has been squared and the 2 has been dropped.

mcqs.stem: 0.50 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Which working gives the thermal energy transferred?

options.rationale: The final temperature has been used instead of the temperature change.
The starting temperature has been used as the temperature change.
∆E = m c ∆θ uses the 60 °C temperature change.
The mass has been left in grams instead of kilograms.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its period?

options.text: 250 s, because period and frequency match
options.rationale: The period is given the same value as the frequency.

options.text: 0.004 s, since period is 1 over the frequency
options.rationale: period = 1/frequency = 1/250 = 0.004 s.

options.text: 500 s, since period is twice the frequency
options.rationale: Period and frequency are assumed to rise together.

options.text: 0.04 s, from 1 divided by only 25 hertz
options.rationale: A place value has been lost from the frequency.

mcqs.stem: How much energy is needed to melt 0.25 kg of ice at 0 °C? The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 334 000 J/kg.

options.rationale: The mass has been left out, so the latent heat itself has been quoted.
The latent heat has been divided by the mass instead of multiplied by it.
A place value has been lost from the specific latent heat.

mcqs.stem: A sample has a volume of 500 cm³. What value should be substituted for V in ρ = m/V to give a density in kg/m³?

options.rationale: The number has been kept and the unit simply relabelled.
The volume has been divided by 1000, as if converting a length.
1 m³ is 1 000 000 cm³, so 500 cm³ is 0.0005 m³.
The decimal point has been moved by only two places.
